chapters.title: Magna Carta (1215)
paragraphs: John greets his archbishops, his bishops and abbots, his earls and barons, his judicial officers and forest officers, his sheriffs, stewards and servants, and every bailiff and subject who owes him loyalty. Through God’s grace he reigns as England’s king, as Ireland’s lord, as duke in Normandy and in Aquitaine, and as Anjou’s count. Let everyone know that we have made the grants set out here out of regard for God, to secure salvation for ourselves, for our ancestors and for our heirs, to honour God, to advance holy Church and to reform our kingdom. We have acted with advice from our revered fathers: Stephen, the archbishop at Canterbury, who is primate for all England and a cardinal serving the holy Roman Church; Henry, the archbishop at Dublin; and these bishops: William of London, together with Peter of Winchester; Jocelyn of Bath and Glastonbury, together with Hugh of Lincoln; Walter of Worcester, together with William of Coventry and Benedict of Rochester. Our advisers also include master Pandulf, a subdeacon whose service is in the household belonging to our lord the Pope, and brother Aymeric, master for England of the order called the Knights of the Temple. We have also consulted these distinguished men: William Marshal, who is earl at Pembroke; William, who is earl at Salisbury; William, who bears the title earl Warenne; William, who is earl at Arundel; Alan of Galloway, Scotland’s constable; Waren Fitz Gerald, and also Peter Fitz Herbert; Hubert de Burgh, the seneschal in Poitou; Hugh de Neville, and also Matthew Fitz Herbert; Thomas Basset, and also Alan Basset; Philip d’Aubigny, and also Robert of Roppesley; John Marshal, and also John Fitz Hugh; with others who owe us allegiance.

1. Our first grant is to God: this charter confirms, on our own behalf and for all our heirs forever, that England’s church is to enjoy freedom, all its rights intact and all its liberties protected from infringement. We require this promise to be honoured. Our intention can be seen in our grant of free elections, a liberty considered both supremely important and essential to England’s church. We made that grant by our own free choice, under no compulsion, confirmed it in a charter, and obtained approval from our lord Pope Innocent III. before the dispute began between ourselves and the barons. We will honour that freedom and require every future heir of ours to honour it faithfully. We also grant each free man in our realm all the liberties written here. On behalf of ourselves and every future heir, we give those men and their heirs the right to possess these liberties and hold them from us and from our heirs forever.

2. When an earl, a baron or another of our direct tenants owing military service dies, an heir who is already an adult at that death and owes “relief” is to receive the inheritance on paying the traditional charge. The rate for the heir or heirs of an earl is £100 where a complete earl’s barony is inherited. A baron’s heir or heirs likewise pay £100 for a complete barony. A knight’s heir or heirs pay at most 100s. for a complete knight’s fee. Where the obligation is smaller, the payment must also be smaller, following the old custom governing fiefs.
3. But if an heir of any of these people has been a minor under guardianship, he is to receive his inheritance on reaching adulthood without paying either a relief charge or a fine.

4. Anyone acting as guardian of an underage heir’s land may collect only reasonable amounts of produce, customary dues and services. He must neither destroy nor waste its people or goods. If we place such an estate in the care of a sheriff or someone else accountable to us for the income, and that person causes destruction or waste there, we will make him provide compensation. We will then place the estate with two trustworthy and prudent men of that fee. They must account for its income either to us or to the person to whom we assign it. If someone purchases or receives such a guardianship from us and causes destruction or waste on the estate, he will lose the guardianship. It will pass instead to two trustworthy and prudent men of that fief, who must account to us on the terms just described.

5. While the guardian has charge of the estate, he must use its income to maintain the houses, parks, fishponds, pools, mills and everything else belonging to it. Once the heir reaches adulthood, the guardian must return all the land to him, supplied with ploughs and “waynage”, the farming equipment appropriate to the agricultural season, to the extent that the estate’s income can reasonably support.
6. An heir must not be married to someone of a lower social standing. Before any marriage takes place, the heir’s closest blood relatives must be informed of it.

7. When a woman’s husband dies, she is to receive her marriage portion and inheritance promptly and without obstacles. She must pay nothing to obtain her dower, her marriage portion, or the inheritance that she and her husband held when he died. She may continue living in his house for forty days following his death, and her dower must be assigned to her within that period.

8. A widow who wants to continue living unmarried must be allowed to do so, without being forced to take a husband. She must, however, guarantee that if she does marry she will first secure our permission when she holds land from us, or her lord’s permission when she holds land from someone else.

9. We and our bailiffs must not seize land or rental income to collect a debt while the debtor’s movable property is enough to cover what he owes. Nor may his guarantors’ property be seized while the principal debtor can meet the obligation. If the principal debtor cannot pay because he has no means, his guarantors must meet the debt. If they want them, they may take possession of his lands and rents until they have recovered the money they paid on his behalf, unless the principal debtor can establish that he no longer owes that obligation to those guarantors.

10. If someone borrows money from Jews, whether the amount is large or small, and dies before repaying it, interest on that debt must stop while the heir remains a minor, regardless of the lord from whom the heir holds land. If we acquire the debt, we will collect only the principal recorded in the bond.

11. When someone dies owing money to Jews, his wife is to receive her dower without contributing anything towards that debt. Any children he leaves who are still minors must be supplied with necessities suitable to the estate he held. The debt must be paid from what remains, while preserving the services owed to the feudal lords. Debts owed to people other than Jews must be handled in the same way.

12. A scutage, the payment in place of military service, or an aid must not be charged on our kingdom without its common counsel. The exceptions are money for our own ransom, for the knighting of our eldest son, and for one marriage of our eldest daughter; even in these cases the aid must be reasonable. The same rules apply when collecting aids from London.

13. London is to keep all the liberties and free customs it has traditionally enjoyed, on waterways as on land. We also decree and grant that every other city, every borough, every town and every port is to keep all its own liberties and free customs.

14. When the kingdom’s common counsel is needed to assess scutage, or an aid outside the three exceptions already listed, we will summon each archbishop, bishop, abbot, earl and greater baron by an individual letter. The sheriffs and bailiffs will issue a general summons to all our other direct tenants. The meeting will have a specified location and date, with at least forty days allowed before it takes place. Each summons letter will explain why the meeting is being called. Once this notice has been given, business will go ahead on the specified day with the advice of those who attend, even if some of the people summoned fail to appear.

15. From now on, we will give nobody permission to demand an aid from his free tenants except to pay his own ransom, to have his oldest son knighted, or to marry his oldest daughter once. Any aid demanded for one of these occasions must be reasonable in amount.
16. Property must not be seized to force the holder of a knight’s fee, or of any other free holding, to perform more service than that particular holding owes.
17. Lawsuits between subjects must be heard at a settled location instead of travelling with our royal court as it moves about.

18. Inquiries into recent dispossession, known as novel disseisin, into inheritance following an ancestor’s death, known as mort d’ancestor, and into a dispute over the last appointment to a church benefice, known as darrein presentment, are to be heard only in their own county courts. This is how they will proceed. We will send two judges to each county on four occasions yearly; if we are outside the kingdom, our chief judicial officer will send them. Four local knights selected by the county will join those judges in hearing these assizes at the usual county court, on its regular meeting day and in its regular meeting place.

19. When the county court cannot hear all these assizes on its meeting day, enough of the knights and freeholders who attended that day must remain to make the necessary judgments properly. How many remain must depend on the amount of work still to be dealt with.

20. A free man’s monetary penalty for a minor offence must match the seriousness of that offence. A serious offence must bring a correspondingly serious penalty, but his “contenement”, his means of maintaining his position, must always be preserved. The same rule applies to a merchant, whose “merchandise” must be preserved, and to a villein, whose “wainage”, his farming resources, must be preserved, if they have incurred our discretionary punishment. None of these monetary penalties may be imposed without sworn testimony from honest local men.
21. Only their peers may impose monetary penalties on earls or barons, and those penalties must be proportionate to the offence committed.
22. A cleric’s monetary penalty relating to his secular holding must follow the rules already given for the others. The value of his church benefice must not be used to assess that penalty.
23. Neither a village nor an individual may be forced to build a bridge at a riverbank unless an established legal obligation to do that work already applies to them.
24. Cases reserved to our Crown must not be heard by sheriffs, by constables, by coroners or by any other bailiffs serving us.

25. The administrative districts—counties, hundreds, wapentakes and trithings—must continue paying their customary rents, with no extra charge added; our demesne manors, the estates we hold in our own hands, are the exception.

26. When someone holding a secular fief from us dies, and our sheriff or bailiff produces our open letters summoning payment of a debt the deceased owed us, that official may seize and list movable goods found on the fief up to the value of the debt. Men legally qualified to witness this must be present. Nothing may be taken away until the established debt has been paid to us in full. The remaining goods must be left with the executors to carry out the deceased’s will. If he owed us nothing, all his movable goods must go to his estate, while protecting the reasonable portions due to his wife and children.

27. If a free man dies without making a will, his nearest relatives and friends must distribute his movable property under the church’s oversight. Each creditor’s claim for what the dead man owed must be preserved.
28. A constable or any other bailiff acting for us must pay immediately when taking anyone’s grain or other supplies. Payment may be delayed only if the seller gives permission for that delay.

29. A constable must not force a knight to pay instead of guarding a castle when the knight is willing to perform the duty himself, or, if a reasonable cause prevents him, through another responsible man. If we have taken or sent the knight on military service, his guard duty must be reduced in proportion to the time he spends serving on our account.
30. A free man’s horses or carts must not be taken for transport work without his agreement, whether by our sheriff, by our bailiff or by anyone else.
31. We must not take someone else’s timber for our castles or any other work of ours without the timber owner’s agreement. The same restriction applies to all our bailiffs.
32. We will keep the lands of a person convicted of felony for no longer than a year plus a day. After that period, the land must pass to the lords of the respective fiefs.
33. From now on, all kydells, the fishing weirs, must be removed completely from the Thames, from the Medway and from everywhere else in England, with the sole exception of the seashore.
34. The writ known as praecipe must no longer be issued to anyone in a case concerning a holding if it would cause a free man to lose jurisdiction in his own court.

35. Wine must have a single standard measure across our entire kingdom, as must ale. Grain must likewise have a single measure, namely “the London quarter”. Cloth, whether dyed cloth, russet or “halberget”, must have one standard width: two ells measured between the selvedges. Weights must be standardised just as measures are.

36. No one may pay or receive a fee for a writ ordering an inquiry in a case involving loss of life or limb. Whenever such a writ is requested, it must be supplied free of charge, and the request must never be refused.

37. Suppose someone holds land from us by fee–farm, socage or burgage, and also holds another lord’s land in return for knight’s service. The fee–farm, socage or burgage tenure gives us no right to guardianship over either his heir or his land belonging to that other lord’s fief. Nor may we take guardianship over the fee–farm, socage or burgage itself, unless that fee–farm owes knight’s service. A minor serjeanty held from us in return for supplying knives, arrows or similar things does not entitle us to guardianship over the tenant’s heir, or over land he holds from another lord in return for knight’s service.

38. A bailiff must no longer make anyone undergo his “law”, the legal means of clearing himself, on the strength of the bailiff’s unsupported accusation alone. Trustworthy witnesses must be produced for that purpose.

39. A free man must not be seized or [and] jailed, deprived of possession, forced into exile or otherwise ruined, nor will we proceed against him ourselves or dispatch others against him, except under a lawful decision delivered by his peers or [and] under the country’s law.
40. We will charge nobody for either justice or right. We will deny neither to anybody, and we will delay neither for anybody.

41. Merchants may enter England safely, leave it safely, stay within it and travel around it by water or over land to buy and sell according to the old and lawful customs, free of every wrongful toll. During wartime, merchants from a country fighting us are excepted. If they are in our country when war begins, they must be held without harm to themselves or their goods until we, or our chief judicial officer, learn how our own merchants found in that enemy country are being treated. If our people are safe there, those foreign merchants must be safe here.

42. People are henceforth legally free to leave our kingdom and come back, travelling safely and securely over land or across water, so long as they keep the loyalty they owe us. During wartime, public policy may require a brief suspension of this freedom. It does not apply to people imprisoned or outlawed in accordance with our kingdom’s law, or to people native to a country fighting us. Merchants are governed by the arrangements already described.

43. Suppose a tenant dies holding land from an escheated barony now in our hands, such as the honour of Wallingford, Nottingham, Boulogne or Lancaster, or any other such barony. His heir must pay us no greater relief charge and perform no additional service beyond what the baron could have required if the barony had stayed with him. Our holding of the barony must be on the same terms as that baron’s holding was.

44. People living outside a forest will no longer have to attend our forest judges in response to a general summons. This exception does not cover those facing proceedings themselves, or those who have guaranteed the appearance of one or more people held for forest offences.
45. Anyone we appoint to serve as a judge, a constable, a sheriff or a bailiff must understand the kingdom’s law and intend to follow it properly.

46. Barons who have founded abbeys and hold royal charters from England’s kings for them, or have held them in long–standing possession, are to exercise their rightful guardianship over those abbeys when they are vacant.
47. Every area declared a forest during our reign must immediately cease to have that status. The same must happen to riverbanks we have placed “in defence”, under restrictions, during our reign.

48. Every abusive custom involving forests, warrens, forest officers, warren keepers, sheriffs and their officers, or riverbanks and their wardens must immediately be investigated within each county. Twelve knights from that county, chosen by its honest men and placed under oath, must conduct the inquiry. Within forty days after the inquiry, those customs must be abolished completely and never brought back. We must first be informed of this, or, when we are outside England, our chief judicial officer must be informed instead.
49. We will promptly return every hostage and charter that Englishmen have handed over to us to guarantee peace or faithful service.

50. We will remove Gerard of Athée’s relatives entirely from their administrative districts, and they are to hold no such office anywhere in England again. They are Engelard of Cigogné; Peter, Guy and Andrew of Chanceaux; Guy of Cigogné; Geoffrey of Martigny and his brothers; Philip Mark, his brothers and his nephew Geoffrey; and their whole brood.

51. Once peace has returned, we will immediately drive out of our realm all knights, crossbowmen, serjeants and hired soldiers born in foreign lands who have brought horses and weapons here to injure the kingdom.

52. If we have taken away anyone’s land, castle, franchise or right without lawful judgment from his peers, we will give it back at once. Any disagreement about that restoration must be decided by the twenty–five barons identified below in the clause guaranteeing peace. Where King Henry, our father, or King Richard, our brother took possessions without that person’s peers having lawfully judged the matter, we may take the standard delay granted to crusaders if we still hold those possessions, or if others hold them and we must guarantee their title. That delay does not apply to a matter already raised in a plea, or investigated on our orders, before we took the cross. Once we return from the expedition, or if we give it up, we will provide full justice without delay in all these cases.

53. We may use that same delay under identical conditions before giving judgment about keeping or removing the forest status of lands designated by Henry, who was our father, or Richard, who was our brother. It also applies to guardianships over another lord’s fief that we have held because its tenant also owed us knight’s service on a fief held from us, and to abbeys founded on other people’s fiefs where the lord of the fee claims a right. When we return from the expedition, or if we abandon it, we will promptly provide full justice to everyone bringing such complaints.
54. Nobody may be taken into custody or put in prison on a woman’s accusation concerning a killing, unless the person killed was her husband.

55. We will cancel completely all fines agreed with us unjustly and contrary to the country’s law, and all monetary penalties imposed unjustly against that law. Otherwise, the matters will be settled by the twenty–five barons specified below in the clause guaranteeing peace, or a majority of those barons, together with Stephen, the previously named archbishop at Canterbury, if he is able to attend, and anyone he chooses to bring along for this work. Business must still go ahead if he cannot attend. If one or more of the twenty–five is involved in a similar case, that baron must take no part in this particular judgment. The remaining members must select replacements solely for deciding this matter, and each replacement must be sworn in.

56. If we have taken land, liberties or anything else from Welshmen in England or Wales without lawful judgment from their peers, we must return it at once. Any dispute about this must be decided in the marches by their peers’ judgment: English holdings under English law, Welsh holdings under Welsh law, and holdings in the marches under the law prevailing there. Welshmen must act on the same terms towards us and our people.

57. Where King Henry, our father, or King Richard, our brother deprived a Welshman of possessions without his peers first reaching a lawful decision, and we still hold those possessions, or others hold them whose title we must guarantee, we may take the customary delay permitted to crusaders. Matters already raised in a plea or investigated on our orders before we took the cross are excepted. As soon as we return, or if we abandon the expedition, we will promptly provide full justice under the laws of the Welsh, with regard to the regions already specified.
58. We will release the son of Llywelyn immediately, along with every hostage from Wales, and give back the charters delivered to us as guarantees that peace would be kept.

59. In returning the sisters and hostages of Alexander, the Scottish king, and dealing with his franchises and rights, we will treat him as we treat our other barons in England. An exception applies if the charters we possess from his father William, the former Scottish king, require something different. His peers in our court will judge how this is to be done.

60. We have promised that, throughout our kingdom, we will respect all the customs and liberties set out here in our relations with our people. Everyone else in the kingdom, whether a member of the clergy or a layperson, must likewise respect them in their own relations with their people.

61. We have made all these concessions for God’s sake, to reform our kingdom and to bring our conflict with the barons more effectively to an end. We want them to enjoy the concessions fully and securely for all time, and therefore provide this guarantee: they may select any twenty–five members of the kingdom’s baronage they wish. Those chosen must do everything in their power to maintain and enforce the peace and the liberties we have granted and confirmed in this charter. If we ourselves, our chief judicial officer, a bailiff or another officer wrong anyone, or breach any provision concerning peace or this guarantee, and four members of the twenty–five learn of the offence, those four must approach us. If we are abroad, they must instead approach our chief judicial officer. They must explain the offence and ask for an immediate remedy. If forty days pass after the notice reaches us without our providing a remedy, or without our chief judicial officer providing one after receiving notice while we are abroad, those four must report the case to the other members. The full body of twenty–five, supported by the community throughout the country, must then put every possible pressure on us. They may occupy our castles, take our land and possessions, and use any other means available until they obtain a remedy they consider sufficient. No bodily harm may be done to us, to the queen or to our children. When the remedy has been obtained, they must return to the relationship they previously had with us. Anyone in the country who wishes may swear to carry out the commands of these barons in implementing every provision here, and may join them in harassing us to the full extent of his ability. We give everyone who wishes open and unrestricted permission to take this oath, and will never forbid anyone to take it. We will order inhabitants who do not voluntarily agree to swear to help the twenty–five constrain and harass us to take the oath on these terms. If a member dies, goes abroad or is otherwise prevented from putting these arrangements into effect, the remaining members must choose someone they consider suitable to replace him, and he must take the same oath as the others. In any business entrusted to them, if all twenty–five are present but disagree, or some have been summoned but refuse or are unable to attend, whatever the majority of those attending decide or command is binding and settled, exactly as if the entire body had agreed. Every member must swear to follow all these provisions faithfully and to do everything within his power to make others follow them. We will seek no measure from anybody, directly or indirectly, that could cancel or reduce any part of these concessions or liberties. If any such measure is obtained, it will have no force or validity, and we will never use it either personally or through somebody else.

62. We completely forgive everyone for all the hostility, hatred and bitterness that have developed between us and our people, both clergy and laypeople, since the dispute began. We also fully pardon and forgive, as far as we are concerned, every offence arising from that dispute, committed by clergy or laypeople between Easter in the sixteenth year of our reign and the return of peace. To confirm this, we have had open letters of testimony prepared for them by lord Stephen, the archbishop at Canterbury, by lord Henry, the archbishop at Dublin, by the bishops already named and by Master Pandulf, concerning this guarantee and the concessions set out above.

63. We therefore declare and firmly require that England’s Church be free, and that the people of our kingdom possess and enjoy every liberty, right and concession already listed. They and their heirs are to hold these from us and our heirs forever, in every place and every respect, as stated earlier, completely and without restriction, freely, undisturbed, properly and peacefully. Both we and the barons have sworn to honour every one of these conditions faithfully and without any malicious intention.

We issue this under our own hand, witnessed by those already named and by many others, at Runnymede’s meadow between the towns of Windsor and Staines, on June the fifteenth, during year seventeen of our reign.
